Senses.Explanation: Does a dog have buddha-nature, or not? The canonical origin is Zhaozhou's own answer-night: he announces the old monk will answer questions tonight, a monk comes out, bows, is judged a brick thrown to fetch jade that fetched only a clod, and asks; Zhaozhou answers No, and when pressed — every being up to the buddhas and down to ants has buddha-nature, why does the dog alone lack it — because karmic consciousness is in him. Wuzu Fayan makes the question his entire hall address and adds one verdict: it also beats a cat a hundred thousand times over. Dahui Zonggao sets it in his catalog of the sickness-proof sayings — what sickness is there in it, in No, in the bamboo comb that offends if named and betrays if not — and Qianyan Yuanzhang orders twelve hours of turning the light around on it: not mind, not buddha, not thing — what is it? The question, then: what is the No? Xueyan Zuqin, lending the ancients' path as second-best expedience, rules that this one No-character is the face before one's parents were born, the knife that cuts the root of birth-and-death dream, the mirror that sees through all past and present difference; Yuansou Xingduan raises both answers — asked once Zhaozhou said No, asked again he said Yes — and rules that if No were final, why the later Yes; if Yes were apt, why the earlier No: catch him here and heaven and earth are yours; Baichi Xingyuan raises the same pair and demands which one is it, where the intent finally rests — see through this and the seven-hundred-twenty-year old Zhaozhou deserves to be called over for a foot-wash; and Hanyue Fazang rules that Zhaozhou only knew setting posts on four hooves and did not know skating on a dog's back — so today he himself skates there, flourishes the whisk, and cries out.
